Claimed that the present grant formula restricting federal contribution to $1,000 and $1,500 per bed, with the proviso that the grant shall not exceed one-third of the total cost, is unsuited to the needs of the province in that it requires, for full utilization of the grant, additional bed construction at an annual rate in excess of financial capacity of the province.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO ORGANIZATION, OFFICERS, ETC.
speechtext: I should like to make a general remark or two with respect to some of the methods employed by those who lend money in small amounts.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO ORGANIZATION, OFFICERS, ETC.
speechtext: Before my friend goes on, may I raise a point of order? This bill does not relate to what are commonly known as small loan companies. It affects only five companies, incorporated under this dominion act, which are under the supervision of the superintendent of insurance. The companies to which this bill relates are not engaged in the small loan business. Their distinguishing characteristic is that they are empowered to , lend on mortgages.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO ORGANIZATION, OFFICERS, ETC.
speechtext:
It happens that the remarks I wish to make apply to companies which are lending money on mortgages. With the permission of the committee I shall proceed for five minutes to develop this subject.
The first point I would make has to do with the misleading advertising put out by those who are lending money. The average man in the street, particularly one who is in urgent need of $100 and cannot get it anywhere except from these people who make small loans, is not usually conversant with rates of interest in tables which would be perfectly clear to a chartered accountant. When these companies say in their advertising that they are prepared to lend, let us say, $100 to a person under certain conditions, they draw up a schedule in which they say that they will lend the sum of $100 and that for this service the borrower will have to pay only the small amount of, let us say, $9 each month for 12 months. That is, if the loan was made on January 1 there would be a payment of $9 at the end of that month; then at the end of February another $9 would be payable. The innocent victim of this type of propaganda, who, I should imagine, thought he was paying eight per cent per annum, actually paid-although I have not figured it out-between twelve and fifteen per cent per annum.

My plea is that legislation should be passed to prevent people from misleading the public in that way. In other words, to put it briefly, when these people advertise that they have money to lend on that basis, they should be made to state clearly in their advertising the amount of interest per cent per annum- note, not just the rate of payment per month, but the interest in terms of percentage per annum.
The second matter to which I should like to refer has reference to money lent on a mortgage, and what I shall say arises from a grievance stated by one of my own constituents. I have looked into the matter and I have found that this grievance represents a fairly general practice. I shall not mention any names, although I am tempted to do so- and I shall do so if the practice continues in my own home town of Saskatoon, from which this complaint came.
This has reference to the borrowing of money for the purchase of a house. In this instance the house was purchased from a perfectly respectable firm, the Toronto General Trust Corporation-and I have nothing to say against them. This lady's lease was expiring, and in a month or so she would have been put out in the street. She went to one of these combined real estate and lending agencies. She had in her possession $2,000 to put down as a cash payment on the purchase of a house, and applied to these agencies for $3,500, the balance of the purchase price, making the total purchase price $5,500. Her job was to get the $3,500 somehow. She could of course obtain it by offering to give a first mortgage to a company that would advance the money.
With that in mind she made a tour of the various agencies in the city. The agency with which she finally did business consented to put up the money and-note this- demanded a bonus of $500 for so doing. So the situation came about that this lady signed a mortgage in favour of that agency for $4,000, on which she pays what I am told is the customary rate of six per cent interest for such a transaction.
She has in her possession a statement signed by a responsible officer of the agency dated March 25, 1948, in the following words:
Purchase price at $5,500, plus bonus of $500; total

She informed me that another agency asked her for a bonus of $700 for similar accommodation. In my view that is a public scandal. Here was a woman who borrowed $3,500 for a perfectly legitimate purpose. I shall be told of course that whether she should sign the mortgage or not was a matter

within her own discretion. But her circumstances, the fact that her lease was expiring, and the further fact that she made her living by keeping boarders, simply meant that she had to sign that mortgage for $4,000 in order to obtain the $3,500. It might be added that her husband is an invalid. The result is that today that woman is paying interest on $4,000 at six per cent. She obtained from the company $3,500, but in addition to paying six per cent on that amount, she is paying six per cent on an additional $500 she never received.
She holds a letter dated April 7 from this same agency in Saskatoon. This appears to be the final word in the matter of closing the transaction-as I shall now close my remarks. This letter states:
The property Is now standing in your name, subject to a mortgage of $4,000 repayable monthly including principal, interest and taxes.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO ORGANIZATION, OFFICERS, ETC.
speechtext: What company pulled a steal like that?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO ORGANIZATION, OFFICERS, ETC.
speechtext: I say people like this should be exposed, and legislation should be passed by the House of Commons to protect innocent victims from such robbery.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO ORGANIZATION, OFFICERS, ETC.
speechtext: What is the name of the company?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO ORGANIZATION, OFFICERS, ETC.
speechtext: I shall give it. This whole transaction has to do with Saskatoon Agencies Limited. It is registered under that name as a company engaged in handling real estate and lending money to victims such as the one I have mentioned. I have mentioned the name of this company because it was concerned with this particular transaction, but there are others.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO ORGANIZATION, OFFICERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, both the points raised by the hon. member for Saskatoon have nothing to do with the companies concerned in this present piece of legislation. No one will decry more than I an instance such as the one last described; but let us always remember that when a person seeks a loan on real estate the amount borrowed must be kept in mind. Many years ago I had a good deal to do with the lending of money on mortgages. I spent my first year as a law student writing out mortgages by hand-they did not allow us to type them in those days. It was felt then that fifty per cent was a safe lendable value. The view was that to that extent, a loan could be made with reasonable safety but that anything over that amount-and in the instance referred to by the hon. member it was a great deal more-involved taking a much greater risk and must bring a greater return. subtopic: PROVISION THAT CORPORATE CROWN AGENCIES MAY SUE AND BE SUED WITHOUT FIAT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have not read this bill, which is perhaps my fault, but I take it that it is the bill that was introduced some time ago by the Minister of Justice to provide that government corporations may sue or be sued in the ordinary courts of the country. I want again to make the plea that I have made for the last six years, that we should be able to sue the government in the same way as we are being allowed under this bill to sue a corporation which it controls. I have never heard from the Minister of Justice, or the last two ministers of justice, any real reason why the subject should not be able to sue this government-or any government; because I am not speaking from the political point of view-without the necessity of obtaining a fiat so to do.
I cannot think it means liberty, I cannot see that it is democratic, that anything of that kind should be necessary. On the last occasion the Minister of Justice told us that there was

Statute Law Amendment no necessity for this because the government had not refused a fiat. He was giving information which he had obtained from his deputy, something that he had heard, but I know that flats have been refused or have been stalled-I use the word in the most respectful sense-so that in the course of getting a fiat a person may become tired and simply let the matter drop.
I can see no legitimate reason why a subject who has been wronged by any government, provincial or otherwise, should have to get a fiat in order to seek redress. This does not apply in connection with our municipal governments. If a city truck runs over me and injures me I can issue a writ, but in most municipalities I would be required to give notice of intention to sue. I am all in favour of that, because the government has agencies in almost every municipality across Canada and I think notice should be given, as is necessary in the case of most municipalities, so that the government could get in touch with its people and have an opportunity of discussing the matter and probably reaching a settlement.
For the subject to have to ask permission to sue is out of date. Of course the thing is based on the old adage that the king can do no wrong. That is the only reason for this silly business of obtaining a flat. If the king can do no wrong, it is obvious that there is no action.
I am not going to move any amendment. As I say, I have raised this question on previous occasions and I am delighted that the minister has gone as far as he has in the direction of granting complete justice to* the subject-or the individual; the latter word is perhaps better, because he does not need to be a subject in order to sue in this country.
Why we are making two bites of the cherry is just beyond me. We should go the whole way, as I think all hon. members believe we should do, and permit the citizen to sue the crown, with the safeguard I have mentioned of giving thirty days' or even sixty days' notice, so that the government, either federal or provincial, may have plenty of time to investigate the matter and probably reach a settlement and thus avoid long and expensive litigation.
I have nothing more to say. I am simply following the course I have taken since I first came here. I can think of no reason why we should continue this antediluvian and outdated idea of insisting on a fiat before the crown can be sued.

of the generous treatment which was accorded the bill the other day I did not feel that I should be so discourteous or ungenerous as to raise a point of order against him. The bill is concerned with the very thing which the hon. member advocates, the abolition of the necessity of a flat in so far as crown companies are concerned.
With regard to the use of fiats in actions by individuals against His Majesty, when the estimates of the Department of Justice are before the committee I shall be glad to go into that matter at whatever length my hon. friend wishes. But with your permission, Mr. Chairman. I should like to say just a word or two by way of reply to my hon. friend in connection with this matter of securing fiats.
To listen to my hon. friend, or to read certain criticisms of the fiat system, one would think that the necessity of getting a fiat placed some great and expensive impediment in the way of people seeking justice against the crown. I am sure that the hon. member for Calgary West knows that the Petition of Right Act is a short and simple statute consisting of fourteen sections. I do not know of a judicature act in any other country that is as short and simple. It provides that where John Doe, we will say, thinks he has some kind of claim against His Majesty, he goes to his solicitor, and the solicitor draws up form A, which is set out in the Petition of Right Act. I should like to refer to form A to show how complicated and difficult-of course I am speaking ironically-it is to file; because I defy my hon. friend or any other member of the house to find a simpler form in any statute of any other country in the world.

Oh, yes, but not more so. When the petition is signed it is taken to the office of the Secretary of State and filed without fee. When the fiat is issued, the Secretary of State upon payment of 'the court fee of $2, will file the petition in the exchequer court, and then the case is before the court. I make these remarks to place the plain facts of this system before members of the house in order that they may judge whether this method is open to all the harsh criticisms that have been made about it from time to time.
On another occasion when my estimates are before the house I shall be glad to go into this other question which is not relevant under this measure, and draw a distinction on the one hand between this bill, which applies to crown corporations, and the retention, on the other hand of the fiat system so far as individual suits against His Majesty, the government, are concerned.
While I am on my feet, having regard to the fact that it was not necessary for me to make a statement about the principles of this bill on second reading, I think it might be desirable before we begin consideration of the individual sections for me to make a brief statement concerning the principle applicable to all such sections.
In recent years, in the preparation of government legislation to incorporate commercial crown companies, it has been the policy and the practice of the government to include in the respective statutes a provision that the corporation so created could sue and be sued in respect of obligations arising out of the business which it conducted. Examples can be given, such as the Industrial Development Bank Act, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act, the Government Companies Operation Act-which is a statute applying to a number of government companies, such as the Polymer Corporation; the Canadian Commercial Corporation Act, the Northwest Territories Power Commission Act, and so on. Unfortunately the practice has been followed only in recent years, and there are a number of statutes of older vintage in which no such provision was included. Unfortunately also the wording of this provision in some of these more recent statutory provisions is not as uniform as it might be, and in some cases the judicial interpretation of some of these provisions has not, in our judgment, always appeared to carry out what seemed to have been the intention of parliament.
We are not adopting any new policy or principle, but in order to carry out a prin-
Statute Law Amendment ciple which has already been adopted by the government we submit the present bill to make the provision uniform for all corporations carrying on commercial business that crown corporations should be suable in the courts without a fiat. The purpose also is to remove any doubts that have arisen in connection with judicial decisions.
The bill passed through the house the other day with such rapidity-and I must thank hon. members for their generous co-operation-that it has resulted in an unintended embarrassment to me. We wanted to have the bill passed at the present session if at all possible, and have been under some pressure in its preparation in order that that object might be accomplished. We were awaiting consideration of one of the sections by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. After second reading of the bill that corporation submitted a change in wording which, after consideration, we commend to the house. I should like to refer hon. members to section 12. I choose this section merely because it deals with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, although hon. members will see that the amendments provided in all other sections are uniform with that provided in section 12.
So far as the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is concerned, hon. members will see that the relevant words in section 12 of the bill read as follows:
Actions, suits or other legal proceedings in respect of any right or obligation acquired or incurred by the corporation may be
(a) brought or taken against the corporation, without the governor general's fiat, etc.
In the case of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation-and the same may be true of some of the other corporations-contracts have been taken in the name of His Majesty as represented by the corporation. Mr. Mansur, head of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and his legal adviser, Mr. Linkletter, were inclined to think there might be some slight doubt, if the bill were left in its present form, whether the language would apply to instruments which have been taken in that manner in the name of His Majesty. Inasmuch as the whole purpose of this statute is to make this provision uniform in all these crown corporations, and to remove all doubt in connection with every one of them, we have agreed to accept the suggestion that after the word "corporation" in the third line the words "on behalf of His Majesty, whether in its name or in the name of His Majesty" should be added. Therefore I have had an amendment prepared making this language applicable to every section of the act and to every one of the corporations

Indian Act INDIAN ACT

subtopic: FUNDS AND EXPENDITURES, ETC.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) moved
subtopic: FUNDS AND EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 267, respecting Indians.
He said: Mr. Speaker, at confederation, pursuant to section 91 of the British North America Act, Indians and lands reserved for Indians and the administration of Indian affairs, which had been under the management of the several provinces, came under control of the parliament and government of Canada. Prior to 1876 there were several acts with respect to Indians which were consolidated in that year, and since then there has been only one Indian Act and one Indian administration in Canada.
The last complete revision of the Indian Act was in 1880, a biblical life span ago, and while it has been amended from time to time, it became increasingly apparent in the light of present day conditions and the stage of development of the Indians that many provisions of the present act were outmoded and did not sufficiently provide the framework within which the needs and aspirations of our Indian population could best be met.
The scope of Indian legislation, past and present, covers many subjects, dealing as it does with practically the whole life of the people living on Indian reserves, including a number of nomadic groups scattered throughout the country, and numbering in all approximately 136,000 at the present time. Here I might mention that the popular conception that the Indians are disappearing is not correct. Actually they are increasing, and during the past decade the rate of increase has been about one and one-half per cent per year. Without taking up too much time it is only possible to touch lightly upon some of the more important subjects covered in the bill, such as band or tribal membership; the selection, purchase and management of Indian reserves; the lease and sale of resources for the benefit of the Indians; the management of Indian trust funds; the administration of estates; the education of Indian children and adults; the election of chiefs and councillors and their powers, and many other related matters.
In recent years considerable thought and study has been given to the problems of the Indians by parliament, the government and various groups, including of course the Indians themselves, throughout Canada. It will be recalled that in 1946 a special joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons was appointed to examine and consider the Indian Act and to report on Indian
TMr. Speaker.]
administration in general. During the sessions of 1946, 1947 and 1948 briefs were received and evidence heard by the committee from representatives of Indian organizations and bands, departmental officials, and other groups and individuals interested in the welfare of the Indians.
I should like to compliment the committee on the fulness of the examination, the wide range and diversity of views and outlook which received attention, and the constructiveness of the recommendations made. The recommendations of the committee, together with the voluminous record of evidence and briefs, have been of great value in the preparation of this bill to give effeot to the changes considered necessary to meet the needs of Indians today. If the house will permit me, I should like to mention particularly the joint chairmen, the hon. member for Essex West (Mr. Brown) and the Hon. William H. Taylor, who, representing the Senate, succeeded the late Hon. J. Fred Johnston; and the late John R. MacNicol, all of whom made the Indians' case their own.
In considering the whole question of Indian legislation it must be remembered that there are a great many Indian tribes widely scattered throughout Canada, speaking different languages, all differing in racial and cultural backgrounds, and in various stages of economic and social development.
In view of these varied and diverse Indian interests, a comprehensive Indian Act has to be broad enough to accommodate the different Indian groups and communities. It was thought therefore that it would be only fair to give the Indians an opportunity to consider the bill, before its enactment into law, as intimated by the Prime Minister on May 5. This has been done, and the representations that have been received from Indian organizations and bands have been given very careful consideration by the government. May I also interject that we are continuing to receive representations, and no doubt will continue to receive them after the bill is passed. I want to assure the house that all these representations will be brought to its attention next session so that any appropriate amendments may be made.
One of the most difficult problems with which Indian administration has been faced is that of determining who is and who is not an Indian. This is a matter in which the Indians themselves are vitally concerned. The present definition of "Indian" has been statutory since 1876, and it was felt that it was not sufficiently clear. In order to clarify the ambiguity, the committee recommended a new definition, and also the revision of existing band membership lists. The committee also recommended that public moneys

appropriated to promote the welfare of Indians should only be spent for the benefit of persons who are legal members of an Indian band. These recommendations have been kept in mind in preparing the bill.
The definition of "Indian" is clarified and made more restrictive. Provision is made for the setting up of an Indian register, in which eventually all Indians will be recorded. Provisional membership lists for approximately eighty-five per cent of the Indian population have been received and are being scrutinized. In keeping with the committee's recommendation that only persons who are in fact Indians should live on reserves and receive moneys appropriated by parliament for the welfare of Indians, provision is made to exclude quarter-bloods born of marriages entered into after the coming into force of this act. No one of quarter-blood status at present living on a reserve would be affected; this would apply only to those children born of marriages contracted after the passing of the act upon reaching the age of twenty-one years.
It is hoped that by clarifying the definition of "Indian", setting up an Indian register and excluding those who are predominantly of non-Indian blood, many of the causes of the complaints that have been voiced by Indians over the right of certain persons to be members of a band and reside on a reserve will be removed. This act, however, will not adversely affect anyone entitled to protection under the present act, and sympathetic consideration will be given to any person whose residence on a reserve has been accepted generally by the band.
The problem of the Indian and of his land, covering as it does every province of Canada, is one of the major responsibilities of the department, and one in which the Indians themselves are vitally concerned. Provision is made in the bill for simplifying and clarifying the procedures to be adopted with respect to the management, surrender, leasing and disposal of Indian reserves and surrendered lands, and to give the Indians, through their elected band councils, greater control over the reserves upon which they reside. These provisions are based upon past experience and present conditions, and are designed to give adequate protection and also provide for the granting of certificates of possession and occupation to individual Indians. Likewise the provisions of the present act dealing with the management of Indian moneys have been simplified, and greater control given to the band council in the expenditure of band funds. The existing provisions with respect to the administration of estates have been completely revised.
Indian Act
Under the present act there are two systems of electing band councils, the one-year and three-year systems for bands in different stages of advancement. It was thought desirable to provide a uniform system of electing chiefs and councillors which would meet the general requirements of Indian bands in all areas in Canada, and by regulation to accommodate varying degrees of social, economic and political development. The bill provides for this. In keeping with the view that Indians should be given every opportunity to participate fully in local affairs and assume greater responsibilities, provision is made for extending the powers of the band council to bring them more into conformity with those ordinarily exercised by municipal authorities.
The exemption from taxation of real and personal property held by Indians on reserves has been modified so that it will not apply to the personal property of Indians ordinarily resident on reserves, other than veterans of the first and second great wars and their wives, who execute a waiver under an amendment to the Dominion Elections Act, 1938; otherwise the exemption from taxation stands as it has stood since this provision was enacted in 1876.
This provision is complementary to the amendment to the Dominion Elections Act passed by the house the day before yesterday. It leaves the matter of voting in federal elections entirely to the voluntary choice of the Indians.
It is proposed to apply this only to personal property; the real property on the reserve is held in trust by the crown and does not belong to the individual Indian, but is held for the use and benefit of the band or community as a whole, and it is felt that such property should not be taxed, as the individual Indian has only an occupational interest in the land.
It may be of interest to note that the Indian Act of 1869 was entitled "An Act for the Gradual Enfranchisement of Indians." At this time it was apparently thought that Indians would become readily absorbed into the general community, and provision was made for any qualified Indian to attain full citizenship by applying for enfranchisement. Since then the way has been open for Indians who have sufficiently demonstrated their ability to maintain themselves off reserves to attain all the rights and privileges enjoyed by other citizens of the country. The procedure is by order in council. Since yearly records were established in 1918, more than 5,000 Indians have sought and received enfranchisement.	.

Indian Act
Indians can be enfranchised either as individuals or by entire bands on their own application or in certain circumstances, and subject to adequate safeguards, on the initiative of the government.
Provision is -made for the individual Indian to be enfranchised with or without his lands. The usual practice is for the Indian to dispose of his lands to a member of the band. Where a whole band is enfranchised of course the land goes with it.
There is only one case of an entire Indian band being enfranchised, and this was in the case of the Wyandots of Anderdon in southwestern Ontario, who were enfranchised oh their own application in the 1880's. The records indicate that this experiment was a success and that the enfranchised Indians took their place in the general community without ill effects and in most cases with beneficial results. The provisions in regard to enfranchisement, while retained as to principle, have been improved for the purpose of facilitating enfranchisement for Indians.
The underlying principles of Indian legislation through the years have been protection and advancement of the Indian population. In the earlier period the main emphasis was on protection. But as the Indians become more self-reliant and capable of successfully adapting themselves to modern conditions, more emphasis is being laid on greater participation and responsibility by Indians in the conduct of their own affairs. Indeed, it may be said that ever since confederation the underlying purpose of Indian administration has been to prepare the Indians for full citizenship with the same rights and responsibilities as those enjoyed and accepted by other members of the community. This aim has not been lost sight of in the preparation of the bill.
The ultimate goal of our Indian policy is the integration of the Indians into the general life and economy of the country. It is recognized, however, that during a temporary transition period of varying length, depending upon the circumstances and stage of development of different bands, special treatment and legislation are necessary.
At the same time it is not claimed that the bill will provide an immediate solution to all the problems of the Indians. The bill is what it purports to be, a revision of the Indian Act based on an appraisal of conditions as they really are and a re-examination of the provisions of the present act in the light of these conditions, a bill which modernizes and improves existing legislation.
If one had been expecting an immediate assimilation of the Indians into all phases

of Canadian life, all that would have been needed would be to repeal the Indian Act, but so long as we have Indians requiring the assistance of the government of Canada in the conduct of their affairs, an Indian Act is necessary to give the government the required statutory authority to expend public money and to do other incidental matters.
However, we have provided for the present and future requirements of the Indian, people by such measures as old age allowances, greater facilities for education such as I detailed to the house last week, and now that the vote in federal elections has been extended to Indians, we hope that increasing numbers of them will take advantage of it and that the business of the Indians will receive additional consideration through elected members in the house representing them. Aside altogether from the desirability of having everyone in Canada vote, this will have the great advantage of leading to more widespread attention to Indian affairs and better administration.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad that a bill to revise the Indian Act has finally come before parliament, but I am sorry it has come in at this time in the session, when, in my opinion, there is no time to give it the consideration which it should have. Moreover, since its introduction some two weeks ago, and its first reading-the motion today is for second reading-there has not been sufficient time for the Indians across the country to consider the provisions of the bill, to study them and to make recommendations as a result of that study.
The Indians throughout Canada, a number of us here in the house, and other persons and associations throughout Canada who have been interested in the Indians and their welfare and the improvement of their situation generally, have been pressing for several years for a revision of the Indian Act.
The minister gave something of an historical review of what has occurred in that respect during the past five or six years. In 1945 we had a full day's debate on Indian affairs as a result of a resolution I moved that the old age pension should be extended to the Indians. At the end of that day's debate the then minister, Mr. Glen, announced that a full-scale revision of the Indian Act would be undertaken, and that a committee of the house would be set up in the following session to get that work under

Indian Act
way. As a result of that undertaking a joint committee of the other place and of this house was set up in 1946. It held sessions throughout that year, and also in 1947 and in 1948. As a result of that study the committee made a draft revision of the Indian Act, and submitted that draft in 1948. That was two years ago. Apparently it has taken the government two years to revise the draft act which was submitted by the committee, and to bring in the present bill.
In view of this long delay it would seem that the government did not consider it a very urgent matter that the Indian Act should be revised. I fail to see why now, at the very end of the session, they should suddenly consider it very urgent to get this bill through without full consideration being possible, either by the Indians or by the members of this house.
At the beginning of this session it was indicated in the speech from the throne that this revision of the Indian Act was to be introduced this year. Subsequently several members of the house, including myself, urged that the bill should be introduced early in the session so that the Indians would have an opportunity to know what the provisions were, and to make recommendations in connection with them. That action was not taken. Instead of the bill being introduced at the beginning of this session, as I believe it should have been, so that there would have been ample time for all of these things to be done and for this bill, if necessary-and I this it is necesary-to be considered by a special committee of the house where detailed study could be given to its various provisions, the bill is introduced at the end of the session, when we are all rushing to get the estimates through and to finish the session before the end of this month.

Somebody says "this week". Apart from that altogether, certainly nearly everybody here is hoping that the session will close at the end of the month. That does not give the time required for proper study of this bill by this house and by the other place, and particularly it does not give the opportunity, which should be given, for Indians across the country to study the bill and make their recommendations.
In his statement this morning the minister said that the Indians had been given an opportunity to consider the bill. In my opinion a statement of that kind from the realistic point of view is a joke. It is of course no joke so far as the Indians are concerned that that position should be taken. But the bill which was given first reading 55946-249
two weeks ago was not printed until a day or two after that. I think it finally came out on the ninth or tenth of the month. Copies were then mailed out. I am sure there are many bands of Indians in this country that have not yet received copies. With regard to the particular bands to which copies were sent, I think they were mailed to the superintendents as well as to the agents. There certainly has not been a wide enough distribution of the bill or anything like sufficient time for the Indians, most of whom, as hon. members know are illiterate or semi-literate, to comprehend all of its provisions, or to send in any reasonable recommendations in connection with them.
We are now on second reading of the bill, and to the extent that second reading means approval of the general principle that the Indian Act should be revised, I think we are all in agreement. We have been pressing for that; we want the act revised. However, this particular bill-in other words, the revision which has been put before us- contains a large number of things which Indians across the country, many of us here, and other people who have been interested in the subject, do not approve. In short, this is not the bill which it was hoped would be introduced. It does not provide for many of the reforms and improvements which it was hoped would be covered by the new bill when it was introduced.
Seeing that that is the situation I hope that the government will not press second reading through to a conclusion. I hope that when we have had the debate today it will be adjourned and the matter left there and brought up immediately at the beginning of the next session; because I am convinced that it is not reasonable to push this bill through at the present session.
It seems to me that giving second reading to this bill at the present time would not only indicate that we want a revision of the Indian Act; it would indicate that this house has given approval in general to the terms of the present bill, and there are many of us here who cannot do that. Many of us who have been most anxious for a revision of the act cannot subscribe to many of the provisions of this bill. I repeat that I hope the government will not press the measure through, but will allow the matter to stand over until next year, and in the meantime hear the representations of the Indians across the country, and bring in a bill embodying a good many of the recommendations which are made. In other words, give us a more satisfactory bill. Someone says that the

Indian Act
act can be amended afterwards; but I have found that the procedure of having acts amended is always difficult.
This is the first time the act has been revised in toto since it was passed about seventy years ago. Under the circumstances I suggest that after this long period of three-quarters of a century without any major revision, we should do a thorough and complete job now, and not talk about bringing in further amendments next year or the year after to cover up deficiencies in the bill.
This is all the more necessary in view of what was said by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) on May 5 in answer to a question put by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) as to what means were to be given to the Indians to make representations in regard to the bill. At that time the Prime Minister made this statement, as reported at page 2205 of Hansard:
The department felt it had all the information required for the drafting of the legislation, and that it would be desirable that the bill be given first reading and be distributed, and then that a sufficient lapse of time be allowed so that interested chiefs and other members of their bands may see what it contains and make representations.
I draw attention particularly to the suggestion that a sufficient lapse of time after first reading be allowed so that the interested chiefs and other members of their bands might see what the bill contained, and make their representations. The plain truth is that sufficient time to do that has not been allowed. Many Indians have not seen the bill and have not been able to study it and make intelligent representations in respect to it. The Prime Minister added this:
Of course it is legislation in the interests of the Canadian nation, but more particularly for the Indians themselves. If it appeared from their reaction to the bill that they would prefer not to have it adopted at this session but rather to have further discussions with them and further consideration of the legislation, their views would be given sympathetic consideration.
I do not think there is any question that the Indians would prefer to have this bill deferred until the next session of parliament so that they can study it and make representations.
I have received a considerable number of letters and telegrams indicating that that is so. I should like to read a few excerpts from some of them to show the reaction to this bill and the evident effort to push it through hastily at this session. The first of these is a copy of a letter addressed to the minister by Mr. John Laurie, secretary of the Indian Association of Alberta, in which he says this:
We are aware that it Is pressing legislation. We are also aware that it seems to have taken almost two years to the day to frame this bill, and that

two weeks, which includes mail transit, is rather short for almost illiterate Indians to discuss, let alone comprehend, its terms.
May we, therefore, urge that we be given assurance that we shall have an extension, even if the bill must be set over for second reading until next session.
At the same time I received a letter, dated June 13, from Mr. Laurie in connection with the bill, in which he said this:
Just got a copy of bill today. Cannot possibly make decent study in two weeks.
Of course he was not allowed two weeks; he was allowed only about nine days. It continues:
Sections of this bill are straight communist dictatorship, without elements of decent respect for a human being. Sections 5 to 16 inclusive damnable, especially 12 (a) (iv).

I clipped this from the
Montreal Gazette of this morning:
Sixty Indian delegates ask act's deferment.
Ottawa, June 20-Sixty delegates of the North American Indian Brotherhood-some in tribal costume-met Citizenship Minister Harris in the parliament buildings tonight to seek deferment of the new Indian act.
They placed before the minister a petition asking parliament not to enact the Indian bill "in view of the fact that many of the clauses are too detrimental to the best interests of the Indians."
The petition was adopted today in resolution form by the sixty delegates in a hastily called convention held here when the brotherhood received word
that the government had introduced the bill, product of three years of committee study of Indian affairs, in parliament.
The delegates, who will hold another session here tomorrow, came from all provinces except Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. They said delegates could not come from those provinces because of western flood conditions.
What I have said and what I have been allowed to read I think indicates the attitude of the Indians. In view of the statement of the Prime Minister, and the fact that the Indians are apparently opposed to having this bill go through at the present time in its present form, I think the government, as I suggested before, should allow the debate to be adjourned and let the bill stand until next session. If the government presses through the second reading of the bill, then I think the clause by clause study should be deferred. I do not think the majority of us here have been able to give sufficient study to the bill to be in position to consider it properly in committee of the whole.
I am not going to risk being called to order again by referring to specific clauses of the bill, but I should like to say something about what is contained in the bill and to indicate some of the things which I think are wrong with it.
Sections 5 to 16 deal with the definition of Indian, and provide for the registration of Indians. I think these sections will prove particularly troublesome. They appear to indicate an arbitrary determination by legislation of the question who are Indians or who will be Indians in the future. It would exclude a considerable number of persons who have always considered themselves as Indians and who were considered by the bands to be Indians.
This brings up the whole matter of the Macdonald report which was issued in Alberta some years ago. The department undertook to remove from the reserves a considerable number of people who had been living there all their lives and who regarded themselves as Indians. Several hundred people were excluded from the reserve, and in many cases from the only life they had ever known, and from any chance of earning a livelihood. There was much complaint, and the government appointed Mr. Justice Macdonald as a royal commissioner to inquire into the whole matter and make recommendations. Mr. Justice Macdonald went up into the north country where most of these people lived and heard representations from the Indians, from departmental officials and so forth, and then submitted his recommendations. One recommendation was that the majority of the people affected be reinstated to Indian status, but the report was not acted

Indian Act
upon. A small number of these people were readmitted to Indian status, but the great majority were not.
These people consider that an injustice has been done to them and they keep bringing up the question. It was brought up before the joint committee on Indian affairs. It now appears that under these sections of the bill the whole question is to be settled arbitrarily, and these people are excluded and will continue to be excluded. It does not seem to me to be a just and reasonable way of dealing with this problem. It seems to be only one of many problems which are being settled arbitrarily and unjustly by the provisions of this bill.
Then there is a provision that persons who have received half-breed land or money-scrip, and their descendants, are to be denied Indian status. At the time of the Riel rebellion many people who were more or less pure blood Indian, or at least mixed blood; many people who were living with the Indians and for all practical purposes were Indians, took half-breed lands or money-scrip. They then sold it to unscrupulous whites for practically nothing. In many cases they were encouraged to take this scrip so that some white man could get possession of land for very little. Many of the descendants of those people now live in the Indian bands.
There has always been great difficulty in determining whether a man's grandfather or great-grandfather took the scrip, and that difficulty still exists. It was on this basis that a lot of people in northern Alberta who were dealt with in the Macdonald report have been excluded from band membership. It is apparent that the provisions of these sections would exclude from band membership a considerable number of people who have been brought up as Indians, who have lived as Indians all their lives, and who know no other way of life. These people could not be reasonably happy in any other form of life. This is a matter which needs more study and consideration.
Another provision is that the illegitimate children of male Indians shall be excluded from band membership and denied Indian status. This brings up the question of what is illegitimacy. In the past a large number of Indians have not considered it necessary to get a marriage certificate and go through a marriage ceremony according to the white man's custom and law. There has always been a large number of Indians who have married according to the old native custom, and in my opinion those marriages should be looked upon as just as legitimate as any other. It is not realistic to expect an Indian

to secure a marriage certificate as a white man would and go through a marriage ceremony, and his children should not be considered illegitimate. Whether or not that will be the effect of this bill, I do not know. Without a careful definition of illegitimacy, certainly this provision will cause a great deal of hardship among Indians and Indian children.
I should like to deal briefly with the provisions of the bill concerning liquor. As all hon. members probably know, up to the present time liquor has been completely prohibited so far as Indians are concerned. The bill prohibits the possession or consumption of liquor on reserves. Any Indian found in an intoxicated condition on a reserve is subject to fine or imprisonment. On the other hand, where bars and beverage rooms exist, Indians are allowed to enter such premises to drink liquor. What the bill actually provides is a compromise between complete prohibition and the laws governing the consumption of liquor as applied to the white population. In my opinion it is an unworkable compromise. From the practical point of view nothing but trouble will arise from it, and it will be impossible of just enforcement. So far as the Indian population is concerned, it seems to me that you must have either one thing or the other. There must be complete prohibition; otherwise Indians must be put on the same basis as white people and made subject to the same laws and penalties involved in the use of liquor.
If that is done then there should be provision in the bill to enable reserves to hold local option votes if they so desire. If the majority of Indians on a particular reserve want it to be a dry reserve, they should have the opportunity to say so. So far as I can ascertain, the majority of Indians in Alberta are against the removal of prohibition, but in other parts of the country that is not so. There are some Indians who think they should be put on the same basis as the white man, and I think there is a great deal to be said for that point of view in certain localities. As I say, the problem could be solved if Indians were put on the same basis as white men, with provision for local option votes so far as individual reserves are concerned. I am quite certain that the compromise arrangement provided in the bill will not work. In Alberta an Indian will go into a beverage room in a small town and get too much beer. As soon as he sets foot on his reserve he will be in trouble.

The same thing applies to cocktail bars, except that I do not think you will find a great number of Indians coming into cities of a size that have cocktail bars. They will go into the small towns that have beer parlours, and that will apply to a substantial proportion of the entire Indian population.
So far as I have been able to ascertain, there is no provision in the bill for the establishment of a commission to settle the treaty rights of the Indians. There is no provision of any sort to satisfy the Indians so far as their claims under their treaty rights are concerned. One of the sorest points among the Indians is that in their opinion their treaty rights have not been observed. They point to the provisions of the various treaties in which they were concerned, and particularly those which gave them the power to fish and hunt at will. Of course those rights are now severely restricted by provincial hunting and fishing laws. The Indians have never had any compensation for the curtailment of their rights.
There is much doubt as to what the position really is so far as Indian rights are concerned. The practical result is that Indians are constantly being arrested for infractions of provincial game laws, whereas they believe that they have the right to hunt and fish wherever and whenever they please. That is a whole problem in itself, and one which needs to be settled. Until it is settled the Indians will continue to be dissatisfied. From the practical point of view I believe there is no question that we cannot allow the Indians to hunt and fish at any time of the year anywhere they please. Nevertheless there should be some settlement made with them for the abrogation of the rights guaranteed in their treaties.
Another section of the bill makes it illegal for any person to solicit or receive contributions from an Indian for the alleged purpose of improving his lot without the written consent of the minister. If that provision is put into effect I believe it will make it impossible for Indians to form associations. As the present time there are quite a few Indian organizations. There are the Indian Association of Alberta, the Indian Union of Saskatchewan, the Native Brotherhood, the Native Brotherhood of British Columbia, and others. If the provision is passed in its present form it seems to me that Indians will not be permitted to form such organizations unless the minister is agreeable to their existence. That does not appear to be reasonable or democratic. I do not think that Indians should be limited in respect to organizations they may wish to form or to
which they may wish to belong. Of course if you are going to form an organization you must have funds to support it.
In the bill power is taken to enfranchise a particular Indian or a band of Indians against their will if, in the opinion of a committee of three appointed by the minister, it is deemed a desirable thing to do. I do not think that is reasonable. I do not think we should force enfranchisement on an Indian when it means, so far as he is concerned, the loss of certain rights and exclusion from his reserve and from medical and other benefits to which he is entitled. There is no question that this is another provision which certainly should not be passed without a great deal more study being given to it.
Over the past five or six years I believe I have been in as close touch with Indian affairs as any other member of the house. I have not had time to digest the bill and study it properly, and I am certainly not yet in a position to suggest what amendments should be made to particular sections. In addition I have not yet been able to ascertain the reactions of Indians in my own province and their recommendations as to the various provisions of the bill. I believe every other member of the house is in the same or a worse position. Therefore I once more make a plea to the government not to push through second reading of the bill, but if they do, let them not carry it beyond that stage.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe that for years many hon. members of this house have looked forward to the introduction of a much more progressive, more modern and more satisfactory Indian Act than we have had on the statute book. Until the joint committee was set up in the last parliament and sat, partly as a committee and partly as a royal commission, for some three years, only twice since 1867, I believe in 1926 and 1930, had commissions or inquiries under the authority of this house gone into the conditions of Indians. I had looked forward to the introduction of the bill, but I must say that I am disappointed in it. It is not the bill we hoped for. It does not do what the joint committee, in its recommendations, hoped such a bill would do. Very reluctantly, and I mean that word, I am joining with those who are asking the minister to withhold the bill for this session.
I feel that the bill is unsatisfactory. I repeat that it does not do the things the members of the committee hoped would be done. It has some good features, but the bill does not put into effect some of the important suggestions contained in the report of that committee, which incidentally was made on June 22, 1948, exactly two years ago. I had

Indian Act
hoped that something more would be done for education than has been done in this bill. It is true that there is some advance over the provisions of the present Indian Act, but I had hoped that the advance would be much greater. I had hoped that consideration would be given to the wishes of those members of the Indian population who desired not only sectarian schools but non-sectarian schools as well. I believe an Indian should have the right to decide exactly what kind of education his child will have in that regard. It is a privilege we demand for ourselves, and I think it is a privilege the Indians should have. While I readily recognize that the provision of the bill-and I do not want to discuss the clause just now-dealing with the educational system among the Indians where agreements are reached with governments, and so on, is a considerable advance over what we have in the present act, in my opinion it does not go far enough.
Then, as was suggested by the hon. member who has just resumed his seat (Mr. Harkness), I believe more attention should have been paid to the recommendation of the committee as to the setting up of a commission to deal with the ancient treaties made with the Indians. That has been a very sore point with the Indian population of this country for a number of years. So far as I have been able to judge, both from the reading of our history and from documentary evidence, and indeed from some of the old treaties, those treaties have not been observed by this country. In my opinion the Indians today are entitled to a thorough investigation into what has been done with respect to their lands and their rights, with a view to the restoration of those rights, or, where restoration is impossible, proper compensation for that which has been taken from them. That, I think, was in the mind of the committee when it made its recommendations in 1948.
We were hoping, to repeat a phrase that was used at the time, that this bill would be something of a Magna Carta for our Indian population, but it falls far short of that. It is merely an amendment of the act now on the statute book. We had hoped this bill would provide in a definite, certain way for the transition of our Indian population from the position of wardship or trusteeship it now occupies in relation to us, toward the goal of complete citizenship and equality with the rest of the population. So we are disappointed with this bill.
I am not going to deal with the various clauses concerning enfranchisement and so on, because an opportunity will be given to the house to discuss them when we study the bill

in detail. However, I believe any hon. member reading the recommendations of the committee, which will be found in the Journals of this house, volume 84, 1948, at pages 647 to 652, and comparing them with the clauses of this bill, will find that the bill falls far short of what was contemplated by the committee at that time. I know that many of these matters of necessity require consultation with the provinces. I believe it was suggested in the report of the committee that matters dealing with education, health and social services, fur conservation, the development of Indian trap lines, provincial fish and game laws, provincial liquor legislation, the validity of marriages solemnized by Indians on Indian reserves according to tribal customs and ritual, all should be the subject of dominion-provincial conference. The recommendation was that these matters should be placed upon the agenda of the next dominion-provincial conference so that they could be discussed and understandings arrived at before we passed a new Indian Act. That has not been done. I know that in some instances there have been negotiations with the departments concerned, with the departments of education in some of the provinces, the departments of natural resources in others, and so on; but there is no uniform understanding between the provinces and the dominion as to what shall be done in these matters for our Indian population.
I do not propose to deal now with these matters at length. I can quite understand the government may feel that very little good would come out of any delay, so far as hearing further representations is concerned, and I have some sympathy with that point of view. I was not a member of the committee which sat for three years, but I did drop in occasionally to listen to the briefs, the representations and the evidence, and I felt there was no consensus among the Indians who appeared before that committee. It seemed to me that in all probability this house and the government would have to make up their minds from the very conflicting evidence that was submitted to the committee, and I doubt very much whether further representations would bring results which would be different from those we have already had from former representations.
But since this bill is in our opinion unsatisfactory, I think that further opportunity- since the time between the introduction of the bill and its second reading has been so short-might be given for further representations, in the hope that more success would be achieved than was the case in 1946, 1947 and 1948. But my main suggestion is not that. It is that the bill is disappointing. The bill is unsatisfactory in so many particulars and fails to

bring into effect so many of the main recommendations of the committee that I think the house and the government would be well advised to let the matter stand for this session.
One other consideration is this. The house apparently is anxious to bring this session to a close. I must say that I have not a great deal of sympathy with that consideration, even if I myself thought the house might close at the end of this week and have made certain engagements because of that belief. But I have not much sympathy with trying to rush things through. This is a bill which is exceedingly important to a large section of our Indian population, and I think that the suggestions that have been made for delay and opportunities for further discussion should be considered by the minister and a decision made to postpone its enactment this session.

I listened, Mr. Speaker, with considerable interest to the statement the minister made when the bill was first proposed for second reading. He gave a good, plausible-sounding speech that tickled the ears and really made one think that the government had accomplished something in this act. As his first highlight I notice that he said that the old act had not been suitable to the needs and the aspirations of the Indians. While I do not recall that he specifically stated that the new act met the needs and the aspirations of the Indians, he surely strongly implied that it did. The second highlight which impressed me was that he mentioned the fact that it had been the government's desire to make provision for permitting the Indians to give careful consideration to this act. And consequently the act, Mr. Speaker, was actually introduced to this house two whole solid weeks before it was brought in here for second reading! In order to give people over thousands and thousands of miles of Canada, in remote areas, a chance to read and consider it! I must admit that two weeks is almost exorbitant in the provision it makes. I wager that over five-sixths of the Indians never did see this act at all, nor their leaders, in the paltry few days that we have been allowed to have for the Indians to study the act.
The third highlight was this one:	The
Indians were to be given more control of their affairs. I had a deputation of Indians waiting on me yesterday, among whom were some of what I consider to be the most intelligent Indians in Canada. They spent a good deal of time telling me that, as far as they could gather from the act, the act had almost successfully removed all hope of effective control by the Indians of their affairs on their own reserves. Of course on reading the act and explaining it under the
Indian Act
minister's direction, probably we shall be able to see wherein he can justify his case. But I should not be a bit surprised if the Indians were right; because, after all, they have been the victims of the kind of government that Canada has given them now for over seventy years, and they recognize from afar the coming evils.
After I heard the minister's speech, I thought probably I had been deceived in connection with the act; so I went and glanced over the act again in order to make sure that I had really been concentrating on it when I had gone through it the first time. On reading this act I find that I simply cannot justify the minister's optimism by any stretch of the imagination. It is an astonishing thing to me that he should have thought that these fine things he spoke of were embodied in the act. I wonder if somebody else wrote his speech for him without his having read the act. I would not think that would be the case, but the minister is an extremely busy man.
I would say that the act is an entirely negative one. It is apparently designed to govern an inferior and subordinate people and to keep them inferior and subordinate. The first great error which has been committed in dealing with our Indians in Canada has been that of taking it for granted that the Indians were an inferior race and a subordinate race, and that we were going to keep them inferior and to keep them subordinate for nobody knows how long. I think that was a wrong point of view.
In the early days while the land was sparsely settled and people were being protected by a thin red line of mounted police over thousands of miles of area, I can understand that considerable anxiety might have filled the minds of those charged with responsibility with respect to the Indians. They might have desired to keep a fairly firm hand over the Indians; and they might have been quite justified in such a desire. I am not sure. I did not live in those days, although I must say that I came into Canada with my parents in 1892. Things were rather primitive in the area in which we settled in those days. We settled right alongside an Indian reservation. I am not sure that what was done was exactly the right thing or the wrong thing. But certainly if there ever was any cause whatsoever for looking upon the Indians as subordinate and for desiring to keep them so, that cause has now disappeared.
It should be borne in mind that the Indians were not a conquered race. They never were a conquered race in this nation. This nation made a treaty with the Indians on equal terms; and in most cases the Indians who

Indian Act
signed those treaties were perfectly worthy to look the white man straight in the eye and to meet him on equal terms. They were just as intelligent, just as skilful, just as noble, just as brave and strong, and just as effective in every single way. In most cases there never was any thought of conquering the Indians. The Indians made a treaty. The treaty money that we find the Indians obtaining throughout Canada is clear evidence that such was the concept. It is time that everybody in Canada, in his thinking and in his acting-and that the government in their thinking and acting-should go back to the time when the Indian was looked upon as an absolute equal.
When we look upon a good many of the Indians today, if we find it hard to consider them as equals, then I must say that the fault lies entirely with us; because the ancestors of the present Indians were certainly the equals of any white man that ever stepped on Canadian soil. I think there is no successful way of controverting that statement at all.
When the act is apparently a negative one and is designed to keep the Indians inferior and subordinate, that fact alone condemns it as a whole, regardless of what the individual clauses may contain of merit.
When I come to examine the act, as a member of the Indian affairs committee, I find myself deeply disappointed. I spent three years of hard work on that Indian affairs committee, as did the other earnest members who were there. To think that, after all our efforts, the sum total of our reward is this contemptible thing we have before us today makes me wonder if I do not have to struggle to keep my faith in humanity. We were told that we were going to help the Indians to help themselves. I looked into the bill, but up to the present time I am sorry to say that I have found no evidence of anything in the bill to help the Indians to help themselves beyond what we had in the old act.
We were told that we were to build a Magna Carta for the Indians. Well, I fail to find any evidence of any Magna Carta for the Indians. I may have overlooked something, and the minister will have an opportunity of pointing out what I have failed to see, but I think he will do pretty well if he can justify any such high sounding hope as that this bill would be a Magna Carta.

speechtext: I did not say that.
